The ℓ p \ell^{p} -Gaussian-Grothendieck problem with vector spins
Tomas Dominguez

Abstract
We study the vector spin generalization of the ℓ p \ell^{p} -Gaussian-Grothendieck problem. In other words, given integer κ ≥ 1 \kappa\geq 1 , we investigate the asymptotic behaviour of the ground state energy associated with the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick Hamiltonian indexed by vector spin configurations in the unit ℓ p \ell^{p} -ball. The ranges 1 ≤ p ≤ 2 1\leq p\leq 2 and 2 < p < ∞ 2<p<\infty exhibit significantly different behaviours. When 1 ≤ p ≤ 2 1\leq p\leq 2 , the vector spin generalization of the ℓ p \ell^{p} -Gaussian-Grothendieck problem agrees with its scalar counterpart. In particular, its re-scaled limit is proportional to some norm of a standard Gaussian random variable. On the other hand, for 2 < p < ∞ 2<p<\infty the re-scaled limit of the ℓ p \ell^{p} -Gaussian-Grothendieck problem with vector spins is given by a Parisi-type variational formula.



1
Introduction and main results

Given an
N\times N
matrix
A=(a_{ij})
and some
1\leq p<\infty
, the
\ell^{p}
-Grothendieck problem consists in maximizing the quadratic form
\smash{\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}a_{ij}\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}}
over all vectors
\bm{\sigma}=(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{N})\in\mathbb{R}^{N}
with unit
\ell^{p}
-norm,
\smash{\lVert\bm{\sigma}\rVert_{p}^{p}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\lvert\sigma_{i}\rvert^{p}=1}
.
In other words, it involves computing the quantity

\mathrm{GP}_{N,p}(A)=\max\Big\{\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}a_{ij}\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}\mid\sum_{i=1}^{N}\lvert\sigma_{i}\rvert^{p}=1\Big\}.

(1)

In the case
p=2
, this is the maximum eigenvalue of the symmetric matrix
(A+A^{T})/2
. On the other hand, the limiting case
p=\infty
has been extensively studied in the mathematics and computer science literature for its applications to combinatorial optimization, graph theory and correlation clustering
[
1
,
5
,
10
,
14
,
26
]
. The range
2<p<\infty
can be thought of as an interpolation between the spectral and the correlation clustering problems
[
21
]
, while the range
1<p<2
seems to be unexplored in the literature. Finding an efficient algorithm to solve the
\ell^{p}
-Grothendieck problem whenever
p\neq 2
is generally difficult
[
18
,
20
,
24
,
25
,
27
]
, so it is natural to study the
\ell^{p}
-Grothendieck problem for random input matrices first. In fact, it should help understand the typical behaviour of (
1
). This leads to the
\ell^{p}
-Gaussian-Grothendieck problem,

\mathrm{GP}_{N,p}=\max\Big\{\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}g_{ij}\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}\mid\sum_{i=1}^{N}\lvert\sigma_{i}\rvert^{p}=1\Big\},

(2)

where
(g_{ij})
are independent standard Gaussian random variables.

The asymptotic behaviour of (
2
) was studied in great detail in
[
6
]
. It was discovered that the re-scaled limit of (
2
) exhibits significantly different behaviour in the ranges
1\leq p\leq 2
and
2<p<\infty
; in the former, it is proportional to some norm of a Gaussian random variable, and in the latter, it is given by a Parisi-type variational formula. In this paper, we will show that this behaviour persists in the vector spin generalization of (
2
). Our work is motivated and greatly influenced by
[
6
]
; however, new ideas are needed to treat the range
2<p<\infty
. These will be detailed at a later stage, and they will allow us to avoid the key truncation step in
[
6
]
as well as its associated technicalities. Therefore, specializing our arguments to the scalar setting,
\kappa=1
, yields a simpler proof of the main result in
[
6
]
.

Before we describe the vector spin analogue of (
2
), let us mention that another motivation for investigating this optimization problem comes from the study of spin glass models. In the language of statistical physics, the quadratic form
\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}g_{ij}\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}
is known as the Hamiltonian of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) mean-field spin glass model, and the quantity (
2
) corresponds to the ground state energy of the SK model on the unit
\ell^{p}
-sphere. From this perspective, the vector spin generalization of (
2
) which we will study in this paper is very natural; it also appears in the computer-science literature
[
1
,
5
,
14
,
19
,
21
]
when studying the convex relaxation of (
2
).

Let us now describe the vector spin generalization of (
2
) using the notation and terminology of statistical physics. Fix an integer
\kappa\geq 1
throughout the remainder of this paper. The Hamiltonian of the vector spin SK model is the random function of the
N\geq 1
vector spins taking values in
\mathbb{R}^{\kappa}
,

(9)

This identity was mentioned in
[
19
]
, but no proof was given. Combining (
9
) with theorem 1.1 and theorem 1.2 in
[
6
]
will immediately give our main result for
1\leq p\leq 2
.

Theorem 1.1
.

If
1<p<2
, then almost surely,

\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N^{1/p^{*}}}\mathrm{\mathbf{GP}}_{N,p}=2^{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{2}{p}}\big(\E\lvert g\rvert^{p^{*}}\big)^{1/p^{*}},

(10)

where
p^{*}
is the Hölder conjugate of
p
and
g
is a standard Gaussian random variable. On the other hand, if
p=1
or
p=2
, then almost surely,

\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\log N}}\mathrm{GP}_{N,1}=\sqrt{2}=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\mathrm{GP}_{N,2}.

(11)

(27)

In
section

2
, we will show that the constrained Lagrangian (
27
) admits a deterministic limit
L_{p,D}(t)
with probability one, and in
section

4
, we will establish the following asymptotic formula for the unconstrained Lagrangian (
23
).

Theorem 1.2
.

If
2<p<\infty
, then almost surely the limit
L_{p}(t)=\lim_{N\to\infty}L_{N,p}(t)
exists for every
t>0
. Moreover, with probability one,

L_{p}(t)=\sup_{D\in\Gamma_{\kappa}}L_{p,D}(t)=\sup_{D\in\Gamma_{\kappa}^{+}}L_{p,D}(t).

(28)

Subsequently, in
section

5
, we will use the basic properties of convex functions to derive the following key relationship between the limits of (
23
) and (
21
).

Theorem 1.3
.

If
2<p<\infty
, then almost surely the limit
\mathrm{\mathbf{GSE}}_{p}=\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathrm{\mathbf{GSE}}_{N,p}
exists and is given by

\mathrm{\mathbf{GSE}}_{p}=\frac{p}{2}\Big(\frac{p}{2}-1\Big)^{\frac{2}{p}-1}t^{\frac{2}{p}}L_{p}(t)^{1-\frac{2}{p}}

(29)

for every
t>0
.

This result reduces the study of the ground state energy (
21
) to that of the Lagrangian (
27
) with positive definite self-overlaps
D\in\Gamma_{\kappa}^{+}
. The main result of this paper will be a Parisi-type variational formula for the limit
L_{p,D}(t)
of (
27
) when
D\in\Gamma_{\kappa}^{+}
. Together with (
29
), (
28
) and (
21
), this will give a Parisi-type variational formula for the
\ell^{p}
-Gaussian-Grothendieck problem with vector spins when
2<p<\infty
.

Given
D\in\Gamma_{\kappa}^{+}
, we now describe the Parisi-type variational formula for the limit
L_{p,D}(t)
of (
27
). Let us call a path
\pi:[0,1]\to\Gamma_{\kappa}
piecewise linear if there exists a partition
0=q_{-1}\leq q_{0}\leq\ldots\leq q_{r}=1
of
[0,1]
and matrices
(\gamma_{j})_{-1\leq j\leq r}\subset\Gamma_{\kappa}
with

\pi(s)=\gamma_{j-1}+\frac{s-q_{j-1}}{q_{j}-q_{j-1}}(\gamma_{j}-\gamma_{j-1})

(30)

when
s\in[q_{j-1},q_{j}]
for some
0\leq j\leq r
. Denote by
\Pi
the space of piecewise linear and non-decreasing functions on
[0,1]
with values in
\Gamma_{\kappa}
,

\Pi=\big\{\pi:[0,1]\to\Gamma_{\kappa}\mid\pi\text{ is piecewise linear, }\pi(x)\leq\pi(x^{\prime})\text{ for }x\leq x^{\prime}\big\},

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle=q_{-1}\leq q_{0}\leq\ldots\leq q_{r-1}\leq q_{r}=1,

\displaystyle 0

Notice that any discrete measure
\zeta\in\mathcal{N}^{d}
may be identified with two sequences of parameters

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle=q_{-1}\leq q_{0}\leq\ldots\leq q_{r-1}\leq q_{r}=1,

(37)

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle=\zeta_{-1}\leq\zeta_{0}\leq\ldots\leq\zeta_{r-1}\leq\zeta_{r}<\infty,

(38)

satisfying
\zeta(\{q_{j}\})=\zeta_{j}-\zeta_{j-1}
for
0\leq j\leq r
. Moreover, the sequences (
33
) and (
37
) can be taken to be the same by duplicating values in (
34
) and (
38
) if necessary. We will often abuse notation and write
\zeta
both for the measure and its cumulative distribution function. Given independent Gaussian vectors
z_{j}=(z_{j}(k))_{k\leq\kappa}
for
0\leq j\leq r
with covariance structure

\Cov z_{j}=\gamma_{j}-\gamma_{j-1},

(39)

recursively define the sequence
(Y_{l}^{\lambda,\zeta,\pi})_{0\leq l\leq r}
as follows. Let

Y_{r}^{\lambda,\zeta,\pi}((z_{j})_{0\leq j\leq r})=f_{\lambda}^{\infty}\Big(\sqrt{2}\sum_{j=1}^{r}z_{j}\Big),

(40)

and for
0\leq l\leq r-1
let

Y_{l}^{\lambda,\zeta,\pi}((z_{j})_{0\leq j\leq l})=\frac{1}{\zeta_{l}}\log\E_{z_{l+1}}\exp\zeta_{l}Y_{l+1}^{\lambda,\zeta,\pi}((z_{j})_{0\leq j\leq l+1}).

(41)

This inductive procedure is well-defined by the growth bounds established in
lemma

A.2
. Introduce the Parisi functional,

\Par_{\infty}(\lambda,\zeta,\pi)=Y_{0}^{\lambda,\zeta,\pi}-\sum_{k\leq k^{\prime}}\lambda_{k,k^{\prime}}D_{k,k^{\prime}}-\int_{0}^{1}\zeta(s)\Sum\big(\pi(s)\odot\pi^{\prime}(s)\big)\ud s,

(42)

where
\Sum(\gamma)=\sum_{k,k^{\prime}}\gamma_{k,k^{\prime}}
is the sum of all elements in a
\kappa\times\kappa
matrix and
\odot
denotes the Hadamard product on the space of
\kappa\times\kappa
matrices.
We have made all dependencies on
\kappa,p,t
and
D
implicit for clarity of notation, but we will make them explicit whenever necessary. The following is our main result.

Theorem 1.4
.

If
2<p<\infty
, then for any
D\in\Gamma_{\kappa}^{+}
and every
t>0
,

L_{p,D}(t)=\inf_{\lambda,\zeta,\pi}\Par_{\infty}(\lambda,\zeta,\pi),

(43)

where the infimum is taken over all
(\lambda,\zeta,\pi)\in\mathbb{R}^{\kappa(\kappa+1)/2}\times\mathcal{N}^{d}\times\Pi_{D}
.

We close this section with a brief outline of the paper.
Section

2
will be devoted to the range
1\leq p\leq 2
and will include a proof of
theorem

1.1
. The rest of the paper will focus on the range
2<p<\infty
. In
section

3
, we will use the Guerra-Toninelli interpolation
[
13
,
29
]
and the Gaussian concentration inequality
[
28
,
29
]
to show that the constrained Lagrangian (
27
) admits a deterministic limit. In
section

4
, we show that, in a certain sense, the limit of the constrained Lagrangian depends continuously on the constraint. This continuity result is inspired by lemma 7.1 in
[
6
]
. Unfortunately, lemma 7.1 in
[
6
]
does not extend to the vector spin setting since we can no longer modify overlaps by simply re-scaling spin configurations. To overcome this issue, we will revisit lemma 4 in
[
33
]
, originally designed to prove a vector spin version of the Ghirlanda-Guerra identities
[
12
]
, and we will leverage Dudley’s entropy inequality
[
9
,
35
]
. With this continuity result at hand, we will closely follow section 7 and section 8 in
[
6
]
to prove
theorem

1.2
and
theorem

1.3
. This will be the content of
section

5
and
section

6
. In
section

7
, we will introduce a free energy functional that depends on an inverse temperature parameter
\beta>0
and is asymptotically equivalent to the constrained Lagrangian (
27
) after letting
\beta\to\infty
. For each finite
\beta>0
, a simple modification of the arguments in
[
33
]
, which we will not detail, gives a Parisi-type variational formula for the limit of the free energy functional. This is reviewed in
section

8
. The rest of the paper is devoted to finding a similar Parisi-type variational formula after letting
\beta\to\infty
. This is where our approach differs substantially from that in
[
6
]
. In our attempt to generalize the truncation argument in sections 10-12 of
[
6
]
to the vector spin setting, we discovered that by a careful analysis of the terminal condition (
36
) and its positive temperature analogue, the proof for the scalar,
\kappa=1
, case could be considerably simplified. This simplified proof extended with minor modifications to the vector spin setting and is what we present between
section

9
and
section

11
of this paper. In particular, our arguments can be used to simplify the proof of the main result in
[
6
]
. The careful analysis of the terminal conditions is undertaken in
section

9
. The resulting bounds are combined with the Auffinger-Chen representation
[
4
,
16
]
in
section

10
to compare the Parisi functional (
42
) and its positive temperature counterpart. The specific form of the Auffinger-Chen representation that we use is a higher dimensional generalization of that in
[
6
,
7
]
. The proof of
theorem

1.4
is finally completed in
section

11
. For the reader’s convenience, we have postponed a number of technical estimates to
appendix

A
, and we have included a review of elementary results in linear algebra in
appendix

B
.

It follows by the Gaussian concentration of the maximum that for any
s>0
,

\mathbb{P}\big\{\lvert L_{N,p,D}(t)-\E L_{N,p,D}(t)\rvert\geq s\big\}\leq 2\exp\Big(-\frac{Ns^{2}}{4\tr(D)^{2}}\Big).

Since the right-hand side of this expression is summable in
N
, the Borel-Cantelli lemma implies that

\limsup_{N\to\infty}\lvert L_{N,p,D}(t)-\E L_{N,p,D}(t)\rvert=0

with probability one. It is therefore sufficient to prove that the sequence
(\E L_{N,p,D}(t))_{N}
admits a limit. We will do this through the Fekete lemma by showing that the sequence
(N\E L_{N,p,D}(t))_{N}
is super-additive. This is equivalent to proving that for all integers

The heuristic validity of
theorem

1.2
should now be clear. From (
18
), the self-overlap of any vector spin configuration is a Gram matrix in
\Gamma_{\kappa}
. This means that for every integer
N\geq 1
, the relationship between the unconstrained Lagrangian (
23
) and the constrained Lagrangian (
27
) is

L_{N,p}(t)=\sup_{D\in\Gamma_{\kappa}}L_{N,p,D}(t).

(48)

Formally bringing the limit into the supremum and using the density of positive definite matrices in the space of non-negative definite matrices yields (
28
). To turn this heuristic into a rigorous argument, we will use a compactness argument. This will be done in
section

5
and will require the continuity properties of the constrained Lagrangian (
27
) that we explore in the next section.

4
Continuity of the constrained Lagrangian

In this section we prove that, in a certain sense, the limit of the constrained Lagrangian (
27
) is continuous with respect to the constraint
D\in\Gamma_{\kappa}
by combining lemma 4 in
[
33
]
with the classical Dudley inequality as it is stated in equation (A.23) of
[
35
]
.

Lemma 4 in
[
33
]
was originally designed to modify the vector spin coordinates in the mixed-
p
-spin model in order to prove the matrix-overlap Ghirlanda-Guerra identities. Using these identities, it is then possible to access the synchronization mechanism
[
31
,
32
]
and find a tight lower bound for the limit of the free energy through the Aizenman-Sims-Starr scheme
[
22
,
33
]
. We will apply this lemma for a different purpose, and, as it turns out, we will need a more explicit expression for the constant
L>0
appearing in the upper bound. For our purposes, it will be important that this constant is uniformly bounded for all
D\in\Gamma_{\kappa}
with uniformly bounded trace. We will therefore repeat the proof of this result and carefully track the dependence of constants.

For each
\epsilon>0
and
D\in\Gamma_{\kappa}
denote by
B_{\epsilon}(D)
the open
\epsilon
-neighbourhood of
D
,

B_{\epsilon}(D)=\{\gamma\in\Gamma_{\kappa}\mid\lVert\gamma-D\rVert_{\infty}<\epsilon\},

is precisely the content of lemma 4 in
[
33
]
.

Lemma 4.1
.

Given
0<\epsilon<\kappa^{-2}
,
D\in\Gamma_{\kappa}
, and
R\in B_{\epsilon}(D)
, there exists a matrix
A=A(R)
such that
ARA^{T}=D_{\epsilon}
and

\tr\big((A-I)R(A-I)^{T}\big)\leq C(\tr(D)+1)\sqrt{\epsilon}

(222)

for some constant
C>0
that depends only on
\kappa
.

Proof.

The proof proceeds in two steps: first we reduce the problem to the case when
D=\Lambda
and then we use Gershgorin’s theorem to conclude. For the reader’s convenience, Gershgorin’s theorem has been transcribed as
theorem

B.1
in the appendix.

Step 1: reducing to
D=\Lambda

Let us suppose temporarily that the result holds when
D
is a diagonal matrix. Since
Q
is an orthogonal matrix and the Hilbert-Schmidt norm is rotationally invariant,

\lVert Q^{T}RQ-\Lambda\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lVert R-D\rVert_{\text{HS}}\leq\kappa\epsilon.

We may therefore find a matrix
A(Q^{T}RQ)
with
A(Q^{T}RQ)Q^{T}RQA(Q^{T}RQ)^{T}=\Lambda_{\epsilon}
and

\tr\big((A(Q^{T}RQ)-I)Q^{T}RQ(A(Q^{T}RQ)-I)^{T}\big)\leq C\tr(\Lambda)\sqrt{\epsilon}.

If we set
A=QA(Q^{T}RQ)Q^{T}
, it is easy to see that
ARA^{T}=Q\Lambda_{\epsilon}Q^{T}=D_{\epsilon}
and

\displaystyle\tr\big((A-I)R(A-I)^{T}\big)

\displaystyle=\tr\big(Q(A(Q^{T}RQ)-I)Q^{T}RQ(A(Q^{T}RQ)-I)Q^{T}\big)

\displaystyle\leq C\tr(D)\sqrt{\epsilon}.

The last inequality uses the cyclicity of the trace, the orthogonality of
Q
and the fact that
\tr(D)=\tr(\Lambda)
. This shows that it suffices to prove the result when
D=\Lambda
and
R\in B_{\epsilon}(\Lambda)
.

Step 2: proof for
D=\Lambda

Introduce the matrices
\smash{R_{m}=(R_{k,k^{\prime}})_{k,k^{\prime}\leq m}}
and
\smash{\Lambda_{m}=\diag(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{m})}
consisting of the first
m
rows and columns of
R
and
\Lambda
respectively. Consider the matrix
\smash{\tilde{R}_{m}=\Lambda_{m}^{-1/2}R_{m}\Lambda_{m}^{-1/2}}
. Since
R_{m}\in B_{\epsilon}(\Lambda_{m})
and
\Lambda_{m}
is diagonal with all elements bounded below by
\sqrt{\epsilon}
, it is readily verified that
\lVert\tilde{R}_{m}-I\rVert_{\infty}\leq\sqrt{\epsilon}
. Gershgorin’s theorem implies that all the eigenvalues of
\tilde{R}_{m}
are within
m\sqrt{\epsilon}
from
1
. The assumption
\epsilon<\kappa^{-2}
implies that
\tilde{R}_{m}
is invertible and allows us to define the matrix

B=B(R_{m})=\Lambda_{m}^{1/2}\tilde{R}^{-1/2}_{m}\Lambda_{m}^{-1/2}.

Using the fact that
R_{m}=\Lambda_{m}^{1/2}\tilde{R}_{m}\Lambda_{m}^{1/2}
, it is easy to see that
BR_{m}B^{T}=\Lambda_{m}
and

(B-I)R_{m}(B-I)^{T}=\Lambda_{m}^{1/2}(I-\tilde{R}_{m}^{1/2})^{2}\Lambda_{m}^{1/2}.

Since the eigenvalues of
\tilde{R}_{m}
are within
m\sqrt{\epsilon}
from
1
, so are the eigenvalues of
\tilde{R}_{m}^{1/2}
. Observe that
\smash{\tilde{R}_{m}^{1/2}}
is symmetric and non-negative definite, so it admits an eigendecomposition
\smash{\tilde{R}_{m}^{1/2}=\tilde{Q}_{m}\tilde{\Lambda}_{m}\tilde{Q}_{m}^{T}}
. It follows by the orthogonality of
\tilde{Q}_{m}
that

\lVert I-\tilde{R}_{m}^{1/2}\rVert_{\text{HS}}=\lVert I-\tilde{\Lambda}_{m}\rVert_{\text{HS}}\leq m\lVert I-\tilde{\Lambda}_{m}\rVert_{\infty}\leq\kappa^{2}\sqrt{\epsilon}.

The cyclicity of the trace, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and
lemma

B.3
now give

\displaystyle\tr\big((B-I)R_{m}(B-I)^{T}\big)

\displaystyle=\tr\big(\Lambda_{m}(I-\tilde{R}_{m}^{1/2})^{2}\big)\leq\lVert\Lambda_{m}\rVert_{\text{HS}}\lVert I-\tilde{R}_{m}^{1/2}\rVert_{\text{HS}}^{2}

\displaystyle\leq\kappa^{4}\tr(\Lambda_{m})\epsilon.

Finally, define the matrix
A
by filling all rows and columns of
B
from
m+1
to
\kappa
with zeros. It is clear that
ARA^{T}=\Lambda_{\epsilon}
. If we denote by
T=(R_{k,k^{\prime}})_{k,k^{\prime}\geq m+1}
the matrix consisting of the last
\kappa-m
rows and columns of
R
, then

\displaystyle\tr\big((A-I)R(A-I)^{T}\big)

\displaystyle=\tr\big((B-I)R_{m}(B-I)^{T}\big)+\tr(T)

\displaystyle\leq\kappa^{4}\tr(\Lambda_{m})\epsilon+(\kappa-m)\epsilon+\sum_{k=m+1}^{\kappa}\lambda_{i}

\displaystyle\leq\big(\kappa^{4}\tr(\Lambda)+2\kappa\big)\sqrt{\epsilon}.

We have used the fact that
T\in B_{\epsilon}(\Lambda)
in the second inequality. This completes the proof.
∎

To bound the first of these terms, for each
\epsilon>0
denote by
\mathcal{N}(A,d,\epsilon)
the
\epsilon
-covering number of the set
A\subset(\mathbb{R}^{\kappa})^{N}
with respect to the metric
d
on
(\mathbb{R}^{\kappa})^{N}
, and write
B_{N}
for the Euclidean unit ball in
(\mathbb{R}^{\kappa})^{N}
. Dudley’s entropy inequality and
corollary

4.3
imply that

\displaystyle(I)

\displaystyle\leq C\int_{0}^{CuN^{1/2}\epsilon^{1/8}}\sqrt{\log\mathcal{N}\big(B_{2}^{N}(u),\ud,\delta\big)}\ud\delta

\displaystyle\leq C\int_{0}^{CuN^{1/2}\epsilon^{1/8}}\sqrt{\log\mathcal{N}\big(B_{2}^{N}(u),\lVert\cdot\rVert_{2,2},2^{-2}u^{-3/2}N^{-1/2}\delta^{2}\big)}\ud\delta

\displaystyle\leq C\int_{0}^{CuN^{1/2}\epsilon^{1/8}}\sqrt{\log\mathcal{N}\big(B_{N},\lVert\cdot\rVert_{2,2},2^{-2}u^{-2}N^{-1}\delta^{2}\big)}\ud\delta.

At this point, recall that the covering number of the Euclidean unit ball
B_{N}
in
(\mathbb{R}^{\kappa})^{N}
satisfies

\Big(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\Big)^{N\kappa}\leq\mathcal{N}(B_{N},\lVert\cdot\rVert_{2,2},\epsilon)\leq\Big(\frac{2}{\epsilon}+1\Big)^{N\kappa}

for every
\epsilon>0
. A proof of this bound may be found in corollary 4.2.13 of
[
38
]
. Combining this with a change of variables reveals that

\displaystyle(I)

\displaystyle\leq CN^{1/2}\kappa^{1/2}\int_{0}^{CuN^{1/2}\epsilon^{1/8}}\sqrt{\log(1+8u^{2}N\delta^{-2})}\ud\delta

\displaystyle=CNu\int_{C\epsilon^{-1/16}}^{\infty}\frac{\sqrt{\log(1+\delta)}}{\delta^{3/2}}\ud\delta\leq CNu\int_{C\epsilon^{-1/16}}^{\infty}\frac{\sqrt{\delta^{1/2}}}{\delta^{3/2}}\ud\delta

\displaystyle\leq CNu\epsilon^{1/64}.

(234)

To bound the term
(II)
, notice that for any
x,y>0
,

(x+y)^{p}-x^{p}=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\ud}{\ud t}(x+ty)^{p}\ud t=p\int_{0}^{1}(x+ty)^{p-1}y\ud t\leq py(x+y)^{p-1}.

(235)

In the heuristic proof of

1.2
given at the end of
section

, we used the density of positive definite matrices in the space of non-negative definite matrices to obtain the second equality in (

). When we come to the rigorous proof of this equality, the argument will be more subtle as

does not quite give continuity. We will instead content ourselves with controlling the limit of the constrained Lagrangian (

) for a non-negative definite matrix
D\in\Gamma_{\kappa}
by that for some positive definite matrix in
\Gamma_{\kappa}^{+}
through the following bound.

Proposition 4.5
.

If

, then for each

, every

and all

L_{p,D}(t)\leq L_{p,D+\epsilon I}+C(1+tp)(\tr(D)+1)^{p/2}\epsilon^{1/64}

(341)

for some constant

that depends only on
\kappa
.

The results established in this section together with the arguments in section 7 of
[
6
]
will allow us to give a rigorous proof of
theorem

1.2
. The proof will consist of two key steps. First, we will use
proposition

4.4
to express a version of the Lagrangian (
23
) localized to a ball of fixed but arbitrary radius
u>0
as a supremum of constrained Lagrangians (
27
). Then, we will modify the scaling arguments in section 7 of
[
6
]
to show that the unconstrained Lagrangian (
23
) can be obtained by taking the supremum of these localized Lagrangians over all radii
u>0
. The formula obtained by taking these successive suprema will be equivalent to the first equality in (
28
). As previously mentioned, the second equality will follow immediately from
proposition

4.5
. The purpose of restricting the supremum to positive definite matrices is technical and will be emphasized when we prove
lemma

11.2
.

(342)

defined for each

. If
\Gamma_{\kappa,u}
denotes the set of matrices in
\Gamma_{\kappa}
with trace at most

,

\Gamma_{\kappa,u}=\{D\in\Gamma_{\kappa}\mid\tr(D)\leq u\},

(343)

then (

,

L_{N,p,u}(t)=\sup_{D\in\Gamma_{\kappa,u}}L_{N,p,D}(t).

(344)

A compactness argument similar to that in lemma 3 of
[
33
]
can be used to show that this equality is preserved in the limit.

Proposition 5.1
.

If
2<p<\infty
, then for every
t>0
and
u>0
, the limit

L_{p,u}(t)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\E L_{N,p,u}(t)

exists and is given by

L_{p,u}(t)=\sup_{D\in\Gamma_{\kappa,u}}L_{p,D}(t).

(345)

Moreover, with probability one,
L_{p,u}(t)=\lim_{N\to\infty}L_{N,p,u}(t)
.

The Gaussian concentration inequality implies that the free energy
F_{N}^{\beta}(S)
deviates from its expectation by more than
1/\sqrt{N}
with probability at most
Le^{-N/L}
, where the constant
L
does not depend on
\beta,N
or
S
. We deduce from this that with probability at least
1-Le^{-N/L}
,

F_{N}^{\beta}(B_{2}^{N}(u))\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}+\frac{\log n}{N\beta}+\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\E F_{N}^{\beta}(\Sigma_{\epsilon}(D^{i})).

Letting
\beta\to\infty
and remembering that the
L^{q}
-norm converges to the
L^{\infty}
-norm reveals that with probability at least
1-Le^{-N/L}
,

L_{N,p,u}(t)\leq\frac{2}{\sqrt{N}}+\max_{1\leq i\leq n}L_{N,p,D^{i},\epsilon}(t).

The Borel-Cantelli lemma and
proposition

4.4
now give a constant
C>0
that depends only on
\kappa
with

\limsup_{N\to\infty}L_{N,p,u}(t)\leq\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\big(L_{p,D_{\epsilon}^{i}}(t)+C(1+tp)(\tr(D^{i})+1)^{p/2}\epsilon^{1/64}\big).

Since
\tr(D_{\epsilon}^{i})\leq\tr(D^{i})\leq u
, this can be bounded further by

\limsup_{N\to\infty}L_{N,p,u}(t)\leq\sup_{D\in\Gamma_{\kappa,u}}L_{p,D}(t)+C(1+tp)(u+1)^{p/2}\epsilon^{1/64}.

Remembering that
L_{N,p,D}(t)\leq L_{N,p,u}(t)
for every
N\geq 1
and
D\in\Gamma_{\kappa,u}
, it follows that

\displaystyle\sup_{D\in\Gamma_{\kappa,u}}L_{p,D}(t)

\displaystyle\leq\liminf_{N\to\infty}L_{N,p,u}(t)

\displaystyle\leq\limsup_{N\to\infty}L_{N,p,u}(t)\leq\sup_{D\in\Gamma_{\kappa,u}}L_{p,D}(t)+C(1+tp)(u+1)^{p/2}\epsilon^{1/64}

Letting
\epsilon\to 0
and using the Gaussian concentration of the maximum completes the proof.
∎

(347)

which holds for every
t,u>0
by a change of variables. The absence of such an equality at the level of the constrained Lagrangian (
27
) is the reason we had to develop the results in
section

4
.

For technical reasons, before we start thinking about proving the asymptotic version of (
346
), we will have to upgrade the statement of
proposition

5.1
to show that
L_{p,u}(t)
is the limit of the localized Lagrangian (
342
) with probability one simultaneously over all
t,u>0
. Heuristically, this should not be too surprising. As the maximum of a collection of concave functions, the localized Lagrangian (
347
) is concave in the pair
(u,t)
conditionally on the disorder chaos
(g_{ij})
. Since a concave function is Lipschitz continuous on compact sets, this suggests that
(u,t)\mapsto L_{N,p,u}(t)
should be Lipschitz continuous on compact sets. This continuity would immediately promote almost sure convergence for each
t,u>0
to a convergence with probability one simultaneously over all
t,u>0
. To make this argument rigorous, we will use an
\ell^{2}
-boundedness result of the
N\times N
random matrix

G_{N}=(g_{ij})_{i,j\leq N}.

(348)

Its proof will rely upon Chevet’s inequality as it appears in theorem 8.7.1 of
[
38
]
.

Lemma 5.2
.

There exist constants
C,M>0
such that with probability at least
1-Ce^{-N/C}
,

\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\lVert G_{N}\rVert_{2}\leq M.

(349)

Proof.

Since
\lVert G_{N}\rVert_{2}=\max_{\lVert x\rVert_{2}=1}(G_{N}x,x)
and
\E(G_{N}x,x)^{2}=1
whenever
\lVert x\rVert_{2}=1
, the Gaussian concentration of the maximum gives a constant
C>0
such that with probability at least
1-Ce^{-N/C}
,

\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\lVert G_{N}\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\E\lVert G_{N}\rVert_{2}+1.

If
g
is a standard Gaussian vector in
\mathbb{R}^{N}
, then Chevet’s inequality applied with
T
and
S
equal to the Euclidean unit ball in
\mathbb{R}^{N}
gives an absolute constant
M>0
with

\E\lVert G_{N}\rVert_{2}=\E\max_{\lVert x\rVert_{2}=1}(G_{N}x,x)\leq M\E\lVert g\rVert_{2}.

(350)

We have used the fact that the Gaussian width of the unit ball is
\E\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_{2}=1}(g,x)=\E\lVert g\rVert_{2}
while its radius is one. Finally, Jensen’s inequality reveals that

(\E\lVert g\rVert_{2})^{2}\leq\E\lVert g\rVert_{2}^{2}=N\E\lvert g_{1}\rvert^{2}=N.

Substituting this into (
350
) and redefining the constant
M>0
completes the proof.
∎

Proposition 5.4
.

If
2<p<\infty
, then almost surely

L_{p,u}(t)=\lim_{N\to\infty}L_{N,p,u}(t)

(352)

for every
t,u>0
.

Proof.

By
lemma

5.3
and a simple application of the Borel-Cantelli lemma, for any
0<K_{1}<K_{2}
there exists some constant
M=M(K_{1},K_{2})
such that almost surely

\limsup_{N\to\infty}\lvert L_{N,p,u}(t)-L_{N,p,u^{\prime}}(t^{\prime})\rvert\leq M\big(\lvert u-u^{\prime}\rvert+\lvert t-t^{\prime}\rvert\big)

(353)

for all
u,u^{\prime},t,t^{\prime}\in[K_{1},K_{2}]
. Since
L_{p,u}(t)
is a deterministic quantity, we also have

\lvert L_{p,u}(t)-L_{p,u^{\prime}}(t^{\prime})\rvert\leq M\big(\lvert u-u^{\prime}\rvert+\lvert t-t^{\prime}\rvert\big)

(354)

for all
u,u^{\prime},t,t^{\prime}\in[K_{1},K_{2}]
. By countability of rationals and
proposition

5.1
, we can find a set
\Omega
of probability one where (
353
) holds simultaneously for all rationals
K_{1},K_{2}\in\mathbb{Q}_{+}
and at the same time
L_{p,u}(t)=\lim_{N\to\infty}L_{N,p,u}(t)
for all
u,t\in\mathbb{Q}_{+}
. The triangle inequality implies that for any
u,t>0
and
u^{\prime},t^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Q}_{+}
,

\displaystyle\lvert L_{N,p,u}(t)-L_{p,u}(t)\rvert

\displaystyle\leq\lvert L_{N,p,u}(t)-L_{N,p,u^{\prime}}(t^{\prime})\rvert+\lvert L_{N,p,u^{\prime}}(t^{\prime})-L_{p,u^{\prime}}(t^{\prime})\rvert

\displaystyle\quad+\lvert L_{p,u^{\prime}}(t^{\prime})-L_{p,u}(t)\rvert.

It follows by (
354
) that on the set
\Omega
,

\limsup_{N\to\infty}\lvert L_{N,p,u}(t)-L_{p,u}(t)\rvert\leq 2M\big(\lvert u-u^{\prime}\rvert+\lvert t-t^{\prime}\rvert\big).

Letting
u^{\prime}\to u
and
t^{\prime}\to t
along rational points completes the proof.
∎

In addition to
proposition

5.4
, the proof of
theorem

1.2
will rely on the fact that the
\ell^{p,2}
-norm potential in the definition of the Hamiltonian (
22
) forces the maximizers of this random function to concentrate in a large enough neighbourhood of the origin with overwhelming probability.

lemma

5.2
completes the proof.

Proof (
Theorem

1.2
).

By
lemma

5.5
, there exist constants
C,M>0
such that with probability at least
1-Ce^{-N/C}
,

L_{N,p}(t)=L_{N,p,M/t}(t)

for any
t>0
.
It follows by a simple application of the Borel-Cantelli lemma and
proposition

5.4
that with probability one,

L_{p,u}(t)=\lim_{N\to\infty}L_{N,p,u}(t)\leq\liminf_{N\to\infty}L_{N,p}(t)\leq\limsup_{N\to\infty}L_{N,p}(t)=L_{p,M/t}(t)\leq\sup_{u>0}L_{p,u}(t)

for every
t>0
and
u>0
. Taking the supremum over all
u>0
gives the almost sure existence of
L_{p}(t)
, and invoking
proposition

5.1
shows that

L_{p}(t)=\sup_{u>0}L_{p,u}(t)=\sup_{D\in\Gamma_{\kappa}}L_{p,D}(t).

(356)

To establish the second equality in (
28
), fix a non-negative definite matrix
D\in\Gamma_{\kappa,u}
as well as
0<\epsilon<\kappa^{-2}
. By
proposition

4.5
, there exists a constant
K>0
that depends only on
\kappa
such that

L_{p,D}(t)\leq L_{p,D+\epsilon I}(t)+K(1+tp)(u+1)^{p/2}\epsilon^{1/64}.

It is readily verified that
D+\epsilon I\in\Gamma_{\kappa}^{+}
, so in fact

L_{p,D}(t)\leq\sup_{D\in\Gamma_{\kappa}^{+}}L_{p,D}(t)+K(1+tp)(u+1)^{p/2}\epsilon^{1/64}.

Taking the supremum over all
D\in\Gamma_{\kappa,u}
, letting
\epsilon\to 0
and remembering (
356
) completes the proof.
∎

6
The ground state energy in terms of the Lagrangian

In
section

5
we proved the first noteworthy result of this paper by expressing the unconstrained Lagrangian (
23
) as a supremum of constrained Lagrangians (
27
) in the limit. As we will see in
section

7
and
section

8
, the constrained Lagrangian (
27
) can be understood using the results in
[
33
]

23

21

theorem

1.3

0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle\bm{\rho}\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle\bm{\rho}\hfil$\crcr}}}(t)|\kern-0.43057pt|\kern-0.43057pt|}_{p,2}^{p}=-\frac{tp}{2}L_{N,p}^{\prime}(t).

Rearranging completes the proof.
∎

Lemma 6.3
.

If
2<p<\infty
, then the function
L_{p}(t)
is differentiable on
(0,\infty)
with

L_{p}(t)=-t\Big(\frac{p}{2}-1\Big)L_{p}^{\prime}(t).

(364)

Proof.

Using
theorem

1.2
, fix a realization
(g_{ij})
of the disorder chaos for which
L_{N,p}(t)
converges to
L_{p}(t)
for all
t>0
. Notice that
L_{N,p}
and
L_{p}
are convex functions. In particular, they are continuous everywhere on
(0,\infty)
and differentiable almost everywhere on
(0,\infty)
. If
0<t_{1}<s<t_{2}
are such that
L_{N,p}
is differentiable at
s
, then the convexity of
L_{N,p}
gives

\frac{L_{N,p}(s)-L_{N,p}(t_{1})}{s-t_{1}}\leq L_{N,p}^{\prime}(s)\leq\frac{L_{N,p}(t_{2})-L_{N,p}(s)}{t_{2}-s},

and
lemma

6.2
yields

\frac{L_{N,p}(s)-L_{N,p}(t_{1})}{s-t_{1}}\leq-\frac{L_{N,p}(s)}{(\frac{p}{2}-1)s}\leq\frac{L_{N,p}(t_{2})-L_{N,p}(s)}{t_{2}-s}.

By continuity of
L_{N,p}
and density of the points of differentiability of
L_{N,p}
in
(0,\infty)
, this inequality implies that for all
0<t_{1}<t<t_{2}<\infty
,

\frac{L_{N,p}(t)-L_{N,p}(t_{1})}{t-t_{1}}\leq-\frac{L_{N,p}(t)}{(\frac{p}{2}-1)t}\leq\frac{L_{N,p}(t_{2})-L_{N,p}(t)}{t_{2}-t}.

Letting
N\to\infty
and then letting
t_{1}\nearrow t
and
t_{2}\searrow t
shows that at any point
t\in(0,\infty)
of differentiability of
L_{p}
,

L_{p}^{\prime}(t)=-\frac{L_{p}(t)}{(\frac{p}{2}-1)t}.

(365)

We will now use this equality to show that
L_{p}
is differentiable everywhere on
(0,\infty)
. By convexity of
L_{p}
and theorem 25.1 in
[
34
]
, it suffices to prove that the sub-differential
\partial L_{p}(t)
consists of a single point for every
t>0
. Fix
t\in(0,\infty)
as well as
a\in\partial L_{p}(t)
, and let
(s_{k})
and
(t_{k})
be points of differentiability of
L_{p}
with
t_{k}\nearrow t
and
s_{k}\searrow t
. By definition of the sub-differential,

L_{p}^{\prime}(t_{k})\leq\frac{L_{p}(t)-L_{p}(t_{k})}{t-t_{k}}\leq a\leq\frac{L_{p}(s_{k})-L_{p}(t)}{s_{k}-t}\leq L_{p}^{\prime}(s_{k})

for every integer
k\geq 1
. Letting
k\to\infty
and combining (
365
) with the continuity of
L_{p}
yields

-\frac{L_{p}(t)}{(\frac{p}{2}-1)t}=\limsup_{k\to\infty}L^{\prime}_{p}(t_{k})\leq a\leq\liminf_{k\to\infty}L_{p}^{\prime}(s_{k})=-\frac{L_{p}(t)}{(\frac{p}{2}-1)t}.

This completes the proof.
∎

To leverage this result into a proof of
theorem

1.3
, we must verify the legitimacy of the change of variables used in (
359
). In other words, we must show that
L_{p}^{\prime}(t)
does not vanish on
(0,\infty)
. Our proof will rely upon the properties of the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble discussed in chapter 2 of
[
2
]
. Recall the definition of the random matrix
G_{N}
in (
348
), and notice that the
N\times N
random matrix

\bar{G}_{N}=\frac{G_{N}+G_{N}^{T}}{\sqrt{2}}

(366)

is distributed according to the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble.

(367)

With this in mind, let

denote the
\ell^{2}
-normalized eigenvector associated with the largest eigenvalue
\lambda_{N}^{N}
of the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble
\bar{G}_{N}
. Given
\delta>0
, applying (
367
) to the spin configuration
\smash{\bm{\sigma}_{\delta}=\sqrt{N\delta}v}
reveals that

L_{N,p}(t)\geq\frac{\big(\bar{G}_{N}\bm{\sigma}_{\delta},\bm{\sigma}_{\delta}\big)}{\sqrt{2}N^{3/2}}-t{|\kern-0.43057pt|\kern-0.43057pt|\bm{\sigma}_{\delta}|\kern-0.43057pt|\kern-0.43057pt|}_{p}^{p}=\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{\lambda_{N}^{N}}{\sqrt{N}}-t\delta^{p/2}N^{p/2-1}\lVert v\rVert_{p}^{p}.

By corollary 2.5.4 in
[
2
]
, the eigenvector
v
is equal in distribution to
g/\lVert g\rVert_{2}
for a standard Gaussian random vector
g
in
\mathbb{R}^{N}
. Moreover, by the strong law of large numbers,

N^{\frac{p}{2}-1}\frac{\lVert g\rVert_{p}^{p}}{\lVert g\rVert_{2}^{p}}=\frac{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\leq N}\lvert g_{i}\rvert^{p}}{(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\leq N}\lvert g_{i}\rvert^{2})^{p/2}}\longrightarrow\frac{\E\lvert g_{1}\rvert^{p}}{(\E\lvert g_{1}\rvert^{2})^{p/2}}=\E\lvert g_{1}\rvert^{p}

almost surely. Together with the asymptotics of
\lambda^{N}_{N}
established in theorem 2.1.22 of
[
2
]
, this implies that

L_{p}(t)\geq\sqrt{2}\delta-t\delta^{p/2}\E\lvert g_{1}\rvert^{p}.

Taking
\delta>0
small enough and using the fact that
p>2
shows that
L_{p}
is strictly positive on
(0,\infty)
. Invoking
lemma

6.3
completes the proof.
∎

Proof (

).

Using

, fix a realization

). Subsequently, we will prove that (

) still holds if the limit in

]
gives a Parisi-type variational formula for the limit in

and

of the quenched free energy (

) for each fixed

and

we will study this formula in the limit

in

.

Proposition 7.1
.

If
2<p<\infty
and
t>0
, then

\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\lim_{N\to\infty}L_{N,p,D,\epsilon}(t)=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\lim_{N\to\infty}\E L_{N,p,D,\epsilon}(t)=L_{p,D}(t)

(372)

almost surely.

Proof.

By the Gaussian concentration of the maximum, it suffices to prove that

\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\lim_{N\to\infty}\E L_{N,p,D,\epsilon}(t)=L_{p,D}(t).

(373)

Given
0<\epsilon<\kappa^{-2}
smaller than the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of
D
, the equality
D_{\epsilon}=D
and
proposition

4.4
imply that

\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\limsup_{N\to\infty}\E L_{N,p,D,\epsilon}(t)\leq L_{p,D}(t).

(374)

On the other hand, the Gaussian concentration of the maximum reveals that for every
\epsilon>0
,

L_{p,D}(t)=\lim_{N\to\infty}L_{N,p,D}(t)\leq\liminf_{N\to\infty}L_{N,p,D,\epsilon}(t)=\liminf_{N\to\infty}\E L_{N,p,D,\epsilon}(t).

Letting
\epsilon\to 0
and remembering (
374
) establishes (
373
) and completes the proof.
∎

) exhibits super-Gaussian decay in the range
2<p<\infty
to show that the analogue of the Parisi formula with vector spins proved in
[

]
for compactly supported measures also holds for the free energy functional (

). We will not give any more details than this, and simply content ourselves with stating the asymptotic formula for (

) which we will use between

and
section

to prove
theorem

1.4
.

(582)

Given a path
\pi\in\Pi_{D}
defined by the sequences (
33
) and (
34
), for each
0\leq j\leq r
consider an independent Gaussian vector
z_{j}=(z_{j}(k))_{k\leq\kappa}
with covariance structure (
39
). Define the sequence
\smash{(X_{l}^{\lambda,\alpha,\pi,\beta})_{0\leq l\leq r}}
recursively as follows. Let

X_{r}^{\lambda,\alpha,\pi,\beta}((z_{j})_{0\leq j\leq r})=f_{\lambda}^{\beta}\Big(\sqrt{2}\sum_{j=1}^{r}z_{j}\Big),

(583)

and for
0\leq l\leq r-1
let

X_{l}^{\lambda,\alpha,\pi,\beta}((z_{j})_{0\leq j\leq l})=\frac{1}{\beta\alpha_{l}}\log\E_{z_{l+1}}\exp\beta\alpha_{l}X_{l+1}^{\lambda,\alpha,\pi,\beta}((z_{j})_{0\leq j\leq l+1}).

(584)

This inductive procedure is well-defined by the growth bounds in
lemma

A.1
. Introduce the Parisi functional,

\Par_{\beta}(\lambda,\alpha,\pi)=X_{0}^{\lambda,\alpha,\pi,\beta}-\sum_{k\leq k^{\prime}}\lambda_{k,k^{\prime}}D_{k,k^{\prime}}-\frac{\beta}{2}\sum_{0\leq j\leq r-1}\alpha_{j}\big(\lVert\gamma_{j+1}\rVert_{\text{HS}}^{2}-\lVert\gamma_{j}\rVert_{\text{HS}}^{2}\big).

(585)

Observe that

\displaystyle\sum_{0\leq j\leq r-1}\alpha_{j}\big(\lVert\gamma_{j+1}\rVert_{\text{HS}}^{2}-\lVert\gamma_{j}\rVert_{\text{HS}}^{2}\big)

\displaystyle=\sum_{0\leq j\leq r-1}\int_{q_{j}}^{q_{j+1}}\alpha(s)\frac{\ud}{\ud s}\lVert\pi(s)\rVert_{\text{HS}}^{2}\ud s

\displaystyle=2\int_{0}^{1}\alpha(s)\Sum\big(\pi(s)\odot\pi^{\prime}(s)\big)\ud s,

(586)

where we have abused notation by writing
\alpha
both for the measure and its cumulative distribution function. The Parisi functional may therefore be expressed as

\Par_{\beta}(\lambda,\alpha,\pi)=X_{0}^{\lambda,\alpha,\pi,\beta}-\sum_{k\leq k^{\prime}}\lambda_{k,k^{\prime}}D_{k,k^{\prime}}-\int_{0}^{1}\beta\alpha(s)\Sum\big(\pi(s)\odot\pi^{\prime}(s)\big)\ud s.

(587)

We have made all dependencies on
D,p
and
t
implicit for clarity of notation, but we will make them explicit whenever necessary. The proof of
theorem

1.4
will leverage the following consequence of the main result in
[
33
]
.

Theorem 8.1
.

If
2<p<\infty
, then

\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\lim_{N\to\infty}F_{N,\epsilon}(\beta)=\inf_{\lambda,\alpha,\pi}\Par_{\beta}(\lambda,\alpha,\pi),

(588)

where the infimum is taken over all
(\lambda,\alpha,\pi)\in\mathbb{R}^{\kappa(\kappa+1)/2}\times\mathcal{M}^{d}\times\Pi_{D}
.

This result can be viewed as a positive temperature analogue of
theorem

1.4
. Together with
theorem

7.3
, it essentially reduces the proof of
theorem

1.4
to showing that

\lim_{\beta\to\infty}\inf_{\lambda,\alpha,\pi}\Par_{\beta}(\lambda,\alpha,\pi)=\inf_{\lambda,\zeta,\pi}\Par_{\infty}(\lambda,\zeta,\pi).

(589)

Notice the similarity between the Parisi functionals (
587
) and (
42
). If it were not for the terms
X_{0}
and
Y_{0}
in (
584
) and (
41
), there would be a natural correspondence between these two functionals obtained by setting
\zeta=\beta\alpha
. The proof of (
589
) will therefore consist in showing that, when evaluated at almost minimizers, the terms
X_{0}
and
Y_{0}
in (
584
) and (
41
) differ by a quantity that vanishes as
\beta\to\infty
. To control this difference, we will compare the terminal conditions (
582
) and (
36
) in
section

9
. We will then use the Auffinger-Chen representation
[
4
,
16
]
in
section

10
to translate the bounds on the terminal conditions into control on
X_{0}
and
Y_{0}
. This analysis will be exploited in
section

11
to establish (
589
) and therefore prove
theorem

1.4
. This strategy is considerably different to that in
[
6
]
, where the free energy functional (
579
) is truncated at some level
M>0
. This truncation simplifies much of the analysis for fixed
M>0
, but requires a lot of care when sending
M\to\infty
. By not truncating the free energy, we simplify and shorten the proof of
theorem

1.4
even in the scalar case,
\kappa=1
, studied in
[
6
]
.

9
Comparison of the terminal conditions

In this section we prove quantitative bounds on the difference between the terminal conditions (
582
) and (
36
). Although the analysis in this section uses only elementary concepts, it is the key to proving
theorem

1.4
; the rest of the paper will use tools from the literature to transform the bounds established in this section into a proof of
theorem

1.4
. To alleviate notation, the inverse temperature parameter
\beta>0
, the Lagrange multiplier
\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{\kappa(\kappa+1)/2}
and the parameters
t>0
and
2<p<\infty
will be fixed throughout this section. We will write
C>0
for a constant that depends only on
\kappa
,
p
and
t
whose value might not be the same at each occurrence.

We begin by bounding
\smash{f^{\beta}_{\lambda}}
from above by
\smash{f_{\lambda}^{\infty}}
up to a small error. It will be necessary to make the dependence of these terminal conditions on
t>0
explicit by writing
\smash{f_{\lambda,t}^{\beta}}
and
\smash{f_{\lambda,t}^{\infty}}
.

.

\delta\to 0
completes the proof.
∎

We now turn our attention to bounding
\smash{f_{\lambda}^{\infty}}
from above by
\smash{f_{\lambda}^{\beta}}
up to a small error. Once again, we drop the dependence of these terminal conditions on
t>0
. Through a simple calculation detailed in the proof of
proposition

9.5
, this essentially comes down to bounding the average of the function (
592
) on a cube by its value at the centre of the cube. In other words, we need a type of mean-value property for the function (
592
). There are two main issues to address: the function (
592
) is not necessarily convex and, for technical reasons, we would like this mean-value property on cubes instead of balls. We will deal with the lack of convexity by adding a convex perturbation to (
592
). Replacing balls by cubes will be done by applying Jensen’s inequality to a function defined on a cube of side-length
\delta>0

10
The Auffinger-Chen representation

In this section we extend the Auffinger-Chen stochastic control representation established for
\kappa=2
and Lipschitz terminal conditions in
[
7
]
to the setting of arbitrary integer
\kappa\geq 1
and terminal conditions with sub-quadratic growth such as (
582
) and (
36
). The results in this section will be combined with the bounds obtained in
section

9
to compare the quantities
X_{0}
and
Y_{0}
in (
584
) and (
41
). This will lead to a proof of
theorem

1.4
in
section

11
.

Throughout this section, a constraint
D\in\Gamma_{\kappa}
, an inverse temperature parameter
\beta>0
, a Lagrange multiplier
\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{\kappa(\kappa+1)/2}
, a
\kappa
-dimensional Brownian motion
\bm{W}=(W_{1},\ldots,W_{\kappa})
and
parameters
t>0
and
2<p<\infty
will be fixed. We will also give ourselves a piecewise linear path
\pi\in\Pi_{D}
defined by the sequences (
33
) and (
34
), as well as a discrete probability distribution
\alpha\in\mathcal{M}^{d}
defined by the sequences (
33
) and (
581
). To prove the Auffinger-Chen representation, it will be convenient to replace the Gaussian random vectors
z_{j}
with covariance structure (
39
) appearing in the definition of the Parisi functional (
587
) by a continuous time stochastic process
\bm{B}=(\bm{B}(s))_{s\geq 0}
that plays the same role,

\bm{B}(s)=\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{s}\pi^{\prime}(r)^{\frac{1}{2}}\ud\bm{W}(r).

(781)

Since
\pi^{\prime}(r)=(q_{j}-q_{j-1})^{-1}(\gamma_{j}-\gamma_{j-1})\in\Gamma_{\kappa}
for
r\in(q_{j-1},q_{j})
, this process is well-defined. Moreover, the Ito isometry shows that

\Cov\big(\bm{B}(q_{j})-\bm{B}(q_{j-1})\big)=2\int_{q_{j-1}}^{q_{j}}\pi^{\prime}(r)\ud r=2(\gamma_{j}-\gamma_{j-1}).

(782)

Remembering that

completes the proof.
∎

The Hamilton-Jacobi equation (
785
) is the vector spin analogue of the Parisi PDE
[
29
]
. We now use similar ideas to those in
[
4
,
16
,
29
]
to obtain the vector spin analogue of the Auffinger-Chen representation from (
785
). To overcome the lack of Lipschitz continuity in the terminal condition (
582
), we will rely upon three classical results in stochastic analysis: the Ito formula, the Girsanov theorem and the Novikov condition
[
11
,
17
]
. Given a filtration
\mathcal{F}=(\mathcal{F}_{s})_{0\leq s\leq 1}
, it will be convenient to denote by
\mathcal{A}
the class of admissible control processes,

\displaystyle\mathcal{A}

\displaystyle=\Big\{\bm{v}=(v_{1},\ldots,v_{\kappa})\mid\bm{v}=(\bm{v}(s))_{0\leq s\leq 1}\text{ is progressively measurable }

(786)

\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\text{and }\E\int_{0}^{1}\lVert\bm{v}(s)\rVert_{2}^{2}\ud s<\infty\Big\}

Proposition 10.2
.

If
2<p<\infty
, then there exists a probability space
(\Omega,\mathcal{F}_{1},\mathbb{P})
, a filtration
\mathcal{F}=(\mathcal{F}_{s})_{0\leq s\leq 1}
, a Brownian motion
\bm{W}=(\bm{W}_{s})_{0\leq s\leq 1}
and a continuous adapted process
\bm{X}=(\bm{X}_{s})_{0\leq s\leq 1}
which together form a weak solution to the stochastic differential equation

\ud\bm{X}(s)=2\beta\alpha(s)\pi^{\prime}(s)\nabla\Phi(s,\bm{X}(s))\ud s+\sqrt{2}\pi^{\prime}(s)^{1/2}\ud\bm{W}(s),\,\,\,\bm{X}(0)=0.

(787)

Moreover,

\displaystyle\Phi(0,0)

\displaystyle=\sup_{\bm{v}\in\mathcal{A}}\E\Big[f_{\lambda}^{\beta}\Big(2\int_{0}^{1}\beta\alpha(s)\pi^{\prime}(s)\bm{v}(s)\ud s+\bm{B}(1)\Big)

(788)

\displaystyle\qquad\quad\quad\,\,-\int_{0}^{1}\beta\alpha(s)\big(\pi^{\prime}(s)\bm{v}(s),\bm{v}(s)\big)\ud s\Big]

with the supremum attained by the admissible process
\bm{v}(s)=\nabla\Phi(s,\bm{X}(s))
.

Proof.

To alleviate notation, let
C>0
denote a constant that depends only on
\kappa
,
\lambda
,
\alpha
,
\pi
,
\beta
,
D
,
p
and
t
whose value might not be the same at each occurrence. An induction based on
lemma

A.1
and
lemma

A.3
can be used to show that for any
\smash{(s,\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 2.0mu\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle x\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 2.0mu\textstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\textstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle x\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 2.0mu\scriptstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle x\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 2.0mu\scriptscriptstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle x\hfil$\crcr}}})\in(0,1]\times\mathbb{R}^{\kappa}}
,

\lVert\nabla\Phi(s,\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 2.0mu\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 2.0mu\textstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\textstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle x\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 2.0mu\scriptstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle x\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 2.0mu\scriptscriptstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle x\hfil$\crcr}}})\rVert_{2}\leq C\Big(1+\lVert\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 2.0mu\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle x\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 2.0mu\textstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\textstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle x\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 2.0mu\scriptstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle x\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 2.0mu\scriptscriptstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle x\hfil$\crcr}}}\rVert_{2}^{\frac{1}{p-1}}\Big).

(789)

With this in mind, consider the process
\bm{L}=(\bm{L}(s))_{0\leq s\leq 1}
,

\bm{L}(s)=\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{s}\beta\alpha(r)\pi^{\prime}(r)^{1/2}\nabla\Phi(s,\bm{B}(r))\ud r.

The growth bound (
789
) and the assumption
\frac{1}{p-1}<1
imply that

\E\exp\int_{0}^{1}\lVert\bm{L}(s)\rVert_{2}^{2}\ud s\leq C\E\exp\big(C\sup_{0\leq s\leq 1}\lVert\bm{B}(s)\rVert_{2}^{2}\big)\leq C\E\exp C\big(\sup_{0\leq s\leq 1}\lVert\bm{W}(s)\rVert_{2}^{2}\big),

where the last inequality uses the fact that
\pi^{\prime}
is piecewise constant. Combining this with Doob’s maximal inequality reveals that

\E\exp\int_{0}^{1}\lVert\bm{L}(s)\rVert_{2}^{2}\ud s\leq C\E\sup_{0\leq s\leq 1}\exp C\lVert\bm{W}(s)\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq C\E\exp C\lVert\bm{W}(1)\rVert_{2}^{2}<\infty.

It follows by the Novikov condition that the stochastic exponential
\mathcal{E}(\bm{L})
is a martingale. If we denote by
\mathbb{Q}
the measure under which
\bm{W}
is a Brownian motion and introduce the measure
\ud\mathbb{P}=\mathcal{E}(\bm{L}(1))\ud\mathbb{Q}
, then Girsanov’s theorem implies that

\tilde{\bm{W}}(s)=\bm{W}(s)-\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{s}\beta\alpha(r)\pi^{\prime}(r)^{1/2}\nabla\Phi(s,\bm{B}(r))\ud r

is a
\mathbb{P}
-Brownian motion. Rearranging shows that
\smash{(\bm{B},\tilde{\bm{W}})}
is a weak solution to (
787
). Henceforth, we will write
\smash{\mathcal{F}=(\mathcal{F}_{s})_{0\leq s\leq 1}}
,
\smash{\bm{W}=(\bm{W}_{s})_{0\leq s\leq 1}}
and
\smash{\bm{X}=(\bm{X}_{s})_{0\leq s\leq 1}}
for a filtration, a Brownian motion and a continuous adapted process which together form a weak solution to (
787
). Given
\bm{v}\in\mathcal{A}
, let
\bm{Y}(s)=2\int_{0}^{s}\beta\alpha(r)\pi^{\prime}(r)\bm{v}(r)\ud r+\bm{B}(s)
. By Ito’s formula and the Parisi PDE (
785
),

\displaystyle\ud\Phi

\displaystyle=\Phi_{s}\ud s+2\beta\alpha(s)\big(\nabla\Phi,\pi^{\prime}(s)\bm{v}(s)\big)\ud s+\big(\nabla^{2}\Phi,\pi^{\prime}(s)\big)\ud s+\sqrt{2}\big(\nabla\Phi,\pi(s)\ud\bm{W}(s)\big)

\displaystyle=-\beta\alpha(s)\Big(\big(\pi^{\prime}(s)(\nabla\Phi-\bm{v}(s)),\nabla\Phi-\bm{v}(s)\big)-\big(\pi^{\prime}(s)\bm{v}(s),\bm{v}(s)\big)\Big)\ud s

\displaystyle\quad+\sqrt{2}\big(\nabla\Phi,\pi(s)\ud\bm{W}(s)\big),

where
\Phi
and its derivatives are evaluated at
(s,\bm{Y}(s))
. The growth bound (
789
), the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, the boundedness of
\pi^{\prime}
and the Ito isometry reveal that

\E\int_{0}^{1}\lVert\nabla\Phi(s,\bm{Y}(s))\rVert_{\infty}^{2}\ud s\leq C\big(1+\sup_{0\leq s\leq 1}\E\lVert\bm{Y}(s)\rVert_{2}^{2}\big)\leq C\Big(1+\E\int_{0}^{1}\lVert\bm{v}(s)\rVert_{2}^{2}\ud s\Big)<\infty.

This means that
(\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{s}(\nabla\Phi,\pi(s)\ud\bm{W}(s)))_{s\leq 1}
is a martingale. Together with the non-negative definiteness of
\pi^{\prime}
, this implies that

\E\Phi(1,\bm{Y}(1))-\Phi(0,0)\leq\int_{0}^{1}\beta\alpha(s)\E\big(\pi^{\prime}(s)\bm{v}(s),\bm{v}(s)\big)\ud s

with equality for the process
\bm{v}(s)=\nabla\Phi(s,\bm{X}(s))
. Rearranging gives the lower bound in (
788
). To prove the matching upper bound, it suffices to show that
\bm{v}(s)=\nabla\Phi(s,\bm{X}(s))
belongs to the admissible class
\mathcal{A}
. Fix
0<s\leq r\leq 1
. By the triangle inequality, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and the growth bound (
789
),

\sup_{0\leq s\leq r}\lVert\bm{X}(s)\rVert^{2}_{2}\leq C\Big(1+\int_{0}^{r}\sup_{0\leq s\leq w}\lVert\bm{X}(s)\rVert_{2}^{2}\ud w+\sup_{0\leq s\leq r}\lVert\bm{B}(s)\rVert_{2}^{2}\Big).

(790)

On the other hand, Doob’s maximal inequality and the Ito isometry yield

\E\sup_{0\leq s\leq r}\lVert\bm{B}(s)\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\E\lVert\bm{B}(r)\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq C\tr\int_{0}^{r}\pi^{\prime}(w)\ud w\leq C\tr(D).

(791)

Substituting this into (
790
) and applying Gronwall’s inequality to the resulting bound shows that
\E\sup_{0\leq s\leq 1}\lVert\bm{X}(s)\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq C
. Invoking (
789
) one last time completes the proof.
∎

where
\partial_{s}\Psi
is understood as the right derivative at the points of discontinuity of
\zeta
. An identical argument to that in
proposition

10.2
gives the following weak form of the Auffinger-Chen representation.

Proposition 10.3
.

If
2<p<\infty
, then there exists a probability space
(\Omega,\mathcal{F}_{1},\mathbb{P})
, a filtration
\mathcal{F}=(\mathcal{F}_{s})_{0\leq s\leq 1}
, a Brownian motion
\bm{W}=(\bm{W}_{s})_{0\leq s\leq 1}
and a continuous adapted process
\bm{X}=(\bm{X}_{s})_{0\leq s\leq 1}
which together form a weak solution to the stochastic differential equation

\ud\bm{X}(s)=2\zeta(s)\pi^{\prime}(s)\nabla\Psi(s,\bm{X}(s))\ud s+\sqrt{2}\pi^{\prime}(s)\ud\bm{W}(s),\,\,\,\bm{X}(0)=0.

(795)

Moreover,

\displaystyle\Psi(0,0)

\displaystyle=\sup_{\bm{v}\in\mathcal{A}}\E\Big[f_{\lambda}^{\infty}\Big(2\int_{0}^{1}\zeta(s)\pi^{\prime}(s)\bm{v}(s)\ud s+\bm{B}(1)\Big)

(796)

\displaystyle\qquad\quad\quad\,\,-\int_{0}^{1}\zeta(s)\big(\pi^{\prime}(s)\bm{v}(s),\bm{v}(s)\big)\ud s\Big]

with the supremum attained by the admissible process
\bm{v}(s)=\nabla\Psi(s,\bm{X}(s))
.

We close this section with a moment bound on the weak solution to the stochastic differential equation (
795
) which will allow us to deal with the fact that
proposition

9.5
only holds for bounded values of

\mkern 2.0mu\textstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\textstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr

\hfil\textstyle x\hfil

.

Lemma 10.4
.

If
(\bm{X}(s))_{0\leq s\leq 1}
is a weak solution to (
795
) and
\eta=\max(1+\frac{1}{p-1},\frac{2}{p-1})\in(1,2)
, then

\E\lVert\bm{X}(1)\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq C\Big(1+\lVert\zeta\rVert_{\infty}(1+\lVert\lambda\rVert_{\infty})^{1+\frac{2}{p-2}}\Big)^{\frac{2}{2-\eta}}

(797)

for some constant
C>0
that depends only on
\kappa,p,t
and
D
.

Proof.

To alleviate notation, let
C>0
denote a constant that depends only on
\kappa,p,t
and
D
whose value might not be the same at each occurrence. If
\E\lVert\bm{X}(1)\rVert_{2}^{2}<1
the result is trivial, so assume without loss of generality that
\E\lVert\bm{X}(1)\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq 1
. Introduce the process
\bm{v}(s)=\nabla\Psi(s,\bm{X}(s))
in such a way that

\bm{X}(1)=\int_{0}^{1}2\zeta(s)\pi^{\prime}(s)\bm{v}(s)\ud s+\bm{B}(1).

The triangle inequality and (
791
) reveal that

\E\lVert\bm{X}(1)\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq C\Big(1+\E\Big\lVert\int_{0}^{1}\zeta(s)\pi^{\prime}(s)\bm{v}(s)\ud s\Big\rVert^{2}_{2}\Big).

(798)

With this in mind, fix
1\leq l\leq\kappa
. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality implies that

\displaystyle\Big(\int_{0}^{1}\zeta(s)(\pi^{\prime}(s)\bm{v}(s))_{l}\ud s\Big)^{2}

\displaystyle\leq C\sum_{k=1}^{\kappa}\Big(\int_{0}^{1}\zeta(s)\pi^{\prime}(s)^{1/2}_{lk}\sum_{i=1}^{\kappa}\pi^{\prime}(s)^{1/2}_{ki}v_{i}(s)\ud s\Big)^{2}

\displaystyle\leq C\sum_{k=1}^{\kappa}\int_{0}^{1}\zeta(s)\pi^{\prime}(s)_{lk}^{1/2}\pi^{\prime}(s)_{lk}^{1/2}\ud s

\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\int_{0}^{1}\zeta(s)\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{\kappa}\pi^{\prime}(s)_{ki}^{1/2}v_{i}(s)\Big)^{2}\ud s

\displaystyle\leq C\lVert\zeta\rVert_{\infty}\int_{0}^{1}\zeta(s)\big(\pi^{\prime}(s)\bm{v}(s),\bm{v}(s)\big)\ud s.

Substituting this back into (
798
) yields

\E\lVert\bm{X}(1)\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq C\Big(1+\lVert\zeta\rVert_{\infty}\int_{0}^{1}\zeta(s)\E\big(\pi^{\prime}(s)\bm{v}(s),\bm{v}(s)\big)\ud s\Big).

On the other hand, taking the zero process in
proposition

10.3
shows that

\E\Big[f_{\lambda}^{\infty}(\bm{X}(1))-\int_{0}^{1}\zeta(s)\big(\pi^{\prime}(s)\bm{v}(s),\bm{v}(s)\big)\ud s\Big]=\Psi(0,0)\geq\E f_{\lambda}^{\infty}(\bm{B}(1))\geq 0,

and therefore

\E\lVert\bm{X}(1)\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq C\big(1+\lVert\zeta\rVert_{\infty}\E f_{\lambda}^{\infty}(\bm{X}(1))\big).

(799)

To bound this further, observe that by (
A
) in
appendix

A
and Jensen’s inequality,

\displaystyle\E f_{\lambda}^{\infty}(\bm{X}(1))

\displaystyle\leq C(1+\lVert\lambda\rVert_{\infty})^{1+\frac{2}{p-2}}\Big((\E\lVert\bm{X}(1)\rVert_{2}^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2(p-1)}}+(\E\lVert\bm{X}(1)\rVert_{2}^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}

\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\quad+(\E\lVert\bm{X}(1)\rVert_{2}^{2})^{\frac{1}{p-1}}+1\Big)

\displaystyle\leq C(1+\lVert\lambda\rVert_{\infty})^{1+\frac{2}{p-2}}(\E\lVert\bm{X}(1)\rVert_{2}^{2})^{\eta/2},

where we have used the assumption that
\E\lVert\bm{X}(1)\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq 1
. Substituting this back into (
799
) and again using the fact that
\E\lVert\bm{X}(1)\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq 1
gives

\E\lVert\bm{X}(1)\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq C\Big(1+\lVert\zeta\rVert_{\infty}(1+\lVert\lambda\rVert_{\infty})^{1+\frac{2}{p-2}}\Big)(\E\lVert\bm{X}(1)\rVert_{2}^{2})^{\eta/2}.

Rearranging completes the proof.
∎

11
Proof of the main result

In this section we finally prove
theorem

1.4
. The proof of the upper bound will follow section 12.2 of
[
6
]
. On the other hand, the proof of the lower bound will be considerably shorter and less involved than its one-dimensional analogue in
[
6
]
. In particular, it will leverage the results of
section

9
to avoid the technicalities associated with truncating. Specializing our arguments to the scalar,
\kappa=1
, case gives a shorter and more direct proof of the main result in
[
6
]
when
2<p<\infty
.

Lemma 11.1
.

If
2<p<\infty
,
D\in\Gamma_{\kappa}
and
t>0
, then

L_{p,D}(t)\leq\inf_{\lambda,\zeta,\pi}\Par_{\infty}(\lambda,\zeta,\pi),

(800)

where the infimum is taken over all
(\lambda,\zeta,\pi)\in\mathbb{R}^{\kappa(\kappa+1)/2}\times\mathcal{N}^{d}\times\Pi_{D}
.

Proof.

By
theorem

7.3
, it suffices to show that

\liminf_{\beta\to\infty}\lim_{N\to\infty}F_{N,\beta^{-1}}(\beta)\leq\inf_{\lambda,\zeta,\pi}\Par_{\infty}(\lambda,\zeta,\pi).

(801)

Fix a Lagrange multiplier
\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{\kappa(\kappa+1)/2}
, a piecewise linear path
\pi\in\Pi_{D}
and a discrete measure
\zeta\in\mathcal{N}^{d}
defined by the sequences (
37
) and (
38
). Given an inverse temperature parameter
\beta>0
, introduce the measure

\alpha^{\beta}(s)=\beta^{-1}\zeta(s)\mathbbm{1}_{[0,1)}(s)+\mathbbm{1}_{\{1\}}(s)

on
[0,1]
. It is clear that
\alpha^{\beta}\in\mathcal{M}^{d}
for
\beta
large enough. Moreover,
\smash{\alpha^{\beta}(\{q_{j}\})=\alpha^{\beta}_{j}-\alpha^{\beta}_{j-1}}
for the sequence of parameters (
581
) defined by
\smash{\alpha^{\beta}_{j}=\beta^{-1}\zeta_{j}}
. The Guerra replica symmetry breaking bound in lemma 2 of
[
33
]
implies that

\lim_{N\to\infty}F_{N,\beta^{-1}}(\beta)\leq\Par_{\beta}(\lambda,\alpha^{\beta},\pi)+\beta^{-1}\lVert\lambda\rVert_{1}+L\beta^{-1}.

(802)

for some constant
L>0
independent of
\beta
. To bound this further, recall that by
proposition

Lemma 11.2
.

If

Proof.

and

whose value might not be the same at each occurrence. For each pair

2.0mu\scriptstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle\sigma\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle\sigma\hfil$\crcr}}}-\frac{3\kappa\log 2\delta}{\beta}.

Taking
L=\beta^{m}
and
\delta=\frac{1}{\beta^{(m+1)/2}}
for
m=\frac{K+1}{2-\eta}
and letting
\beta\to\infty
establishes (
823
) and completes the proof.
∎

Appendix B
Background material

In this appendix we collect a number of elementary results from linear algebra.

Theorem B.1

(Gershgorin)
.

If
A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}
and
R_{i}=\sum_{j\neq i}\lvert a_{ij}\rvert
is the sum of the absolute values of the non-diagonal entries in the
i
’th row of
A
, then the eigenvalues of
A
are all contained in the union of the Gershgorin discs,

G(A)=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}\{z\in\mathbb{C}\mid\lvert z-a_{ii}\rvert\leq R_{i}\}.

(B.1)

Proof.

See theorem 6.1.1 in
[
15
]
.
∎

Corollary B.2
.

If
A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}
is a symmetric matrix with non-negative diagonal entries satisfying

a_{ii}=\lvert a_{ii}\rvert\geq\sum_{j\neq i}\lvert a_{ij}\rvert

(B.2)

for
1\leq i\leq n
, then
A
is non-negative definite.

Proof.

In the notation of Gershgorin’s theorem, condition (
B.2
) may be written as
a_{ii}\geq R_{i}
. It follows by the symmetry of
A
and Gershgorin’s theorem that all the eigenvalues of
A
are non-negative. This completes the proof.
∎

Lemma B.3
.

If
A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}
is a non-negative definite and symmetric matrix, then

\lVert A\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}\leq\tr(A).

(B.3)

Proof.

Let
\lambda_{n}\geq\lambda_{n-1}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{1}\geq 0
be the real and non-negative eigenvalues of the matrix
A
.
Since the trace of a matrix is the sum of its eigenvalues,

\lVert A\rVert_{\text{HS}}^{2}=\tr(AA^{T})=\tr(A^{2})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}^{2}\leq\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\Big)^{2}=\tr(A)^{2}.

We have used the fact that the eigenvalues of
A^{2}
are
\lambda_{n}^{2}\geq\lambda_{n-1}^{2}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{1}^{2}\geq 0
in the third equality and the non-negativity of the eigenvalues of
A
in the inequality.
∎

Lemma B.4
.

If
A,B,C\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}
are non-negative definite and symmetric matrices with
B\leq C
, then
\tr(AB)\leq\tr(AC)
. In particular,
\lVert B\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}\leq\lVert C\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}
whenever
B\leq C
.

Proof.

Since
A
is symmetric and non-negative definite, there exists a symmetric and non-negative definite matrix
M
with
M^{T}M=A
. If
M=(m_{1},\ldots,m_{n})
, where
m_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
denotes the
i
’th column of
M
, then

A=M^{T}M=\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_{i}m_{i}^{.}

The linearity and cyclicity of the trace imply that

\tr(AB)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tr(m_{i}m_{i}^{T}B)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tr(m_{i}^{T}Bm_{i})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_{i}^{T}Bm_{i}.

Invoking the assumption that
B\leq C
yields
\tr(AB)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_{i}Cm_{i}^{T}=\tr(AC)
. To complete the proof observe that

\lVert B\rVert_{\text{HS}}^{2}=\tr(B^{T}B)\leq\tr(B^{T}C)=\tr(C^{T}B)\leq\tr(C^{T}C)=\lVert C\rVert_{\text{HS}}^{2},

where we have used the fact that the trace of a matrix coincides with the trace of its transpose.
∎

Lemma B.5
.

If
A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}
is a symmetric and positive definite matrix and
P\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}
is a symmetric matrix, then there exists
\epsilon^{*}=\epsilon^{*}(A,\lVert P\rVert_{\infty},n)>0
such that

A+\epsilon P

(B.4)

is symmetric and positive definite for every
\epsilon<\epsilon^{*}
.

Proof.

Denote by
\lambda_{1}
the smallest eigenvalue of
A
. For any
x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
and every
\epsilon>0
,

x^{T}(A+\epsilon P)x\geq x^{T}Ax-\epsilon\lVert P\rVert_{\infty}\lVert x\rVert_{1}^{2}\geq(\lambda_{1}-\epsilon n\lVert P\rVert_{\infty})\lVert x\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Since
\lambda_{1}>0
by positive definiteness of
A
, setting
\epsilon^{*}=\frac{\lambda_{1}}{n\lVert P\rVert_{\infty}}
completes the proof.
∎
